absent: Compat and native register set layouts and timeval binary layouts are not shown.
Wire encoding of file handles beyond the fid union and length limits is not shown.
Export permission and open hook contracts and name and parent lookup error behavior are not shown.
Fanotify queueing, mark lifecycle, overflow handling and response enforcement are not shown.
Descriptor table resize protocol, RCU grace handling and next descriptor allocation rules are not shown.
File position locking rules and reference counting internals beyond conditional release are not shown.
File reference increment, saturation and release transitions beyond the read mapping are not shown.
Filesystem flag enforcement and extended attribute value ranges are not shown.

findings.text: Each listed header carries a traditional include guard macro that prevents double inclusion and has no behavioral effect beyond that.
A GNU property entry holds a 32-bit type tag followed by a 32-bit data size, with no further fields shown.

The generic ELF header family has two exclusive build variants. One maps the generic header plus program header plus section header plus note plus address plus half-word plus word plus property alignment names to 32-bit forms, while the other maps the same generic names to 64-bit forms.

Compat signal info carries number plus code plus error as compat integers. Compat status common groups that signal info with a short current signal, with pending and held sets as compat unsigned longs, with four compat identifiers for pid and parent and group and session, and with four old 32-bit timevals for user and system and cumulative user and cumulative system clocks.

Compat process info holds four single-byte fields for numeric state and display character and zombie flag and nice value, then a compat flag word with compat user and group identifiers, then four compat process identifiers, then a fixed sixteen-byte executable name plus an argument area sized by the ELF argument constant.
Compat status extends the compat common block with a compat general register set plus an integer flag recording whether floating state is valid.

Native signal info carries number plus code plus error as plain integers. Native status common mirrors the compat shape with native widths: signal info with a short current signal, with native unsigned long pending and held sets, with native pid types, and with kernel old timevals for the four CPU clocks.

Native status pairs the native common block with a native register set plus an integer floating-valid flag. Native process info mirrors compat widths natively: four bytes for state and display and zombie and nice, a native flag word with native user and group identifiers, native pids, a fixed sixteen-byte name, and an argument area.
The initial argument list area exposed in ELF process info holds 80 characters.
The sixteen-byte executable name in both native and compat process info is exposed to userspace and must remain hard coded even though it derives from the task name length.
The Linux link-time optimization info note type has value 0x101.
The build LTO info note is emitted as a 32-bit Linux note of the LTO type whose payload distinguishes two build variants, one carrying one and the other zero.

One note construction family works at assembly level by opening a note section for a given name with caller flags, aligning and recording name size and description size and type plus a terminated name, then closing with trailing alignment and section pop. A convenience wrapper fixes the flags to allocatable and inserts a caller description between open and close.

A second note family builds a uniquely named constant object in the note section for a chosen word size, combining a note header with name bytes and a typed description, each aligned to that word size. Shorthands select the 32-bit and 64-bit word sizes.
An epoll key pairs a file pointer with an integer descriptor and is packed with no padding.
The maximum file handle size is 128.

A file identifier is a union offering a four-word 32-bit inode view, a packed 64-bit inode plus generation view, a block and partition reference view with parent fields, and a flexible raw word array.

Identifier discriminants reserve 0 for root and 0xff for invalid with a warning against filesystem use, use 1 and 2 for 32-bit inode forms, 0x81 and 0x82 for 64-bit forms, and distinct codes for btrfs 0x4d through 0x4f and UDF 0x51 and 0x52 and NILFS 0x61 and 0x62 and FAT 0x71 and 0x72 and Lustre 0x97 and bcachefs 0xb1 and 0xb2 and nsfs 0xf1 and kernfs 0xfe, with paired with-parent and without-parent variants where applicable.

Path resolution from a handle takes a root path with a flag word plus raw handle flags. Supported checks request permission validation on bit 0 and subtree confinement on bit 1. Exported handle creation uses 0x1 for connectable handles carrying parent data, 0x2 for possibly non-decodeable handles, and 0x4 for directory-only decoding.

User visible identifier flag space occupies the upper sixteen bits with mask 0xffff0000. Defined bits are 0x10000 for connectable and 0x20000 for directory, and their combination defines the valid user flag set.

Export operations group callbacks for encoding handles and resolving handles to dentries and parents and for name lookup and parent lookup and metadata commit, plus optional permission and open hooks for path based handles, plus a flag word and an optional block operations pointer when that configuration is enabled.

Filesystems wishing to support export provide entry points for handle encoding and handle-to-dentry and handle-to-parent translation, with optional parent and name lookup and metadata commit and path permission and open hooks invoked by the export layer.

Export option bits are 0x1 for no writeback cache data, 0x2 for no subtree checking, 0x4 for close before unlink, 0x8 for remote filesystem, 0x10 for no atomic attribute updates, 0x20 for flush on close, and 0x40 for no locking support.
A helper reports that locking is unavailable whenever the no-locks export option is set in the operations flag word.
Export for network use is allowed only when handle decoding is supported and neither custom open nor custom permission hooks are present, because network serving does not honor those hooks.
A fid encoding wrapper encodes an inode without a parent while marking the handle as possibly non-decodeable.
Group flag testing inspects the notification data flags of a group for a caller supplied bit.

Permission classes combine content with pre-content. Class bits add notification. Fid reporting combines directory fid with name and target information. Info modes combine fid reporting with pidfd and mount reporting. Admin init flags add permission classes with thread id and pidfd and fd error and unlimited queue and marks, while user init flags allow notification plus fid bits plus mount plus cloexec plus nonblock, and their union forms the full init set.

An internal unprivileged bit sits at 0x80000000 and forms the internal group flag set. Mark type bits cover inode and mount and filesystem and mount namespace. Command bits cover add and remove and flush. Ignore bits cover ignored mask and ignore. The full mark flag set adds dont-follow and only-dir and ignored-survive-modify and evictable.

Path events group access with modify and close and open and exec-open. Dirent events group move with create and delete and rename. Content permission events group open permission with exec-open permission and access permission. Pre-content holds pre-access alone. Permission events unite content with pre-content permission. Descriptor events unite path with permission. Inode events unite dirent with attrib and move-self and delete-self. Error holds filesystem error while mount events hold attach and detach. The general event set unites path with inode plus error plus mount.

Outgoing events unite general and permission events with queue overflow and on-directory. Event flags hold event-on-child with on-directory. Directory-only bits combine dirent events with event-on-child and on-directory, and all event bits unite outgoing with event flags. Responses distinguish allow versus deny access, add audit and info flags, and validate access plus flags plus a shifted errno mask.
The default inline descriptor count equals the number of bits in a machine word.
A descriptor table records a maximum count with a current descriptor array plus close-on-exec and open and full bitmaps plus a reclaim head for deferred freeing.

The open files object holds a reference count with a resize progress flag and wait queue plus an indirection to the current table with an embedded table, followed on a separate cache line by a spinlock with a next descriptor hint and inline close-on-exec and open and full words and an inline descriptor array sized by the default.

The files object splits read-mostly table state reached through an RCU protected pointer from writer state serialized by its file spinlock, with table replacement deferred through RCU and concurrent resizers waiting on the resize queue.
A descriptor range holds two unsigned integers naming lower and upper bounds.
A lightweight descriptor result wraps a single machine word carrying both lookup state and release obligations.
Two release bits are defined with value 1 for reference drop and 2 for position unlock, and the empty value is the all-zero word.

Release drops the file reference only when the reference bit is set, and the positional variant additionally unlocks the file position only when the unlock bit is set before performing the conditional drop.
Taking a descriptor atomically exchanges the slot with a bad-descriptor error marker and returns the prior contents.
Preparation state holds an error word with a reserved descriptor number plus a reserved file pointer that callers must not touch directly.
Cleanup releases the reserved descriptor when non-negative and drops the reserved file unless it is null or an error pointer.
Validation prefers a stored error, then a negative reserved number, then an encoded pointer error, then treats a null file as out of memory, otherwise reports success.

Initialization reserves an unused descriptor with caller flags, attaches a caller owned file on success, and records acquisition status. Addition runs preparation and, when preparation reports success, publishes the reserved slot and returns the publish result.

On 64-bit builds the file reference states use wide unsigned values: zero for one reference, 0x7FFFFFFFFFFFFFFF for maximum, 0xA000000000000000 for saturated, 0xC000000000000000 for released, 0xE000000000000000 for dead, and all ones for no reference.
On other builds the same six reference states use narrow unsigned values: zero, 0x7FFFFFFF, 0xA0000000, 0xC0000000, 0xE0000000, and 0xFFFFFFFF.
The reference object wraps a 64-bit atomic counter on 64-bit builds and a plain atomic counter otherwise.
Reading reports zero whenever the raw count lies at or above the released threshold, otherwise it reports raw count plus one.

Reference counts progress from the one-reference encoding through bounded increments toward maximum, then into saturated and released and dead marker zones with no-reference as a distinct terminal encoding. Reads collapse the released zone and above to zero.
Counts that reach saturated or beyond must be treated as non-dereferenceable, with reads reporting zero rather than a large value.
Common attribute flags group sync with immutable and append and nodump and noatime and dax and project-inherit and verity, with a parallel extended flag grouping.

Read-only extended bits cover prealloc with hasattr and verity and casefold and case-nonpreserving. Value bits cover extsize and cow-extsize. Directory-only bits cover rt-inherit and no-symlinks and extsize-inherit. Miscellaneous bits cover realtime and nodefrag and filestream. The full mask is the union of common with read-only plus values plus directory-only plus miscellaneous.

Kernel attributes hold a legacy flag word with extended flags and extsize and nextents and project identifier and cow-extsize, plus two one-bit selectors recording whether legacy and extended sides are valid.
Extended state counts as present only when the extended valid selector is set and at least one non-common extended flag or a nonzero extsize or project or cow-extsize is present.
External atomic long read used to sample the file reference counter.
External error-pointer test used when validating prepared file state.
External null-or-error test used when cleaning up prepared file state.
External error extraction used when reporting a prepared file pointer failure.
